parts.note: reads as a warhorse, but means one who brings a charge against someone in court

explanation.walkthrough: A charger is usually a cavalry horse; here it is a person who charges, that is, lays an accusation.
explanation.definitionFit: One who charges another with a crime is a prosecutor or complainant: the one bringing the accusation.

parts.note: reads as a wonderful name, but means the name belonging to Marvell, the poet of To His Coy Mistress

explanation.walkthrough: 'Marvellous' means belonging to Marvell: the 17th-century poet's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The English poet Marvell, author of To His Coy Mistress, had this as his Christian name.

clue.text: Fly-fish on a Gallic isle in Spain

parts.note: to fly-fish is to cast a line
ile is the French word for island

explanation.surface: An angler fly-fishing off a small French island, oddly placed in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gallic' points to French: ILE is the French island.
explanation.definitionFit: The old central kingdom, a region of Spain around Madrid, lies within that country.

parts.note: sounds like diplomatic tangles in a parliament called a Diet, but describes tangled strands of Italian pasta on the menu

explanation.walkthrough: A Diet is a parliament, as in Japan, so the surface is about international politics; the second reading is tangled strands of Italian pasta in what one eats.
explanation.definitionFit: Long thin pasta from Italy twists into knots on the plate, foreign food that tangles in one's daily fare.

parts.note: the saying goes that virtue is its own reward, so it receives no payment beyond itself

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'virtue is its own reward' implies that virtue gets no other payment.
explanation.definitionFit: Repaid or rewarded; the proverb says virtue earns nothing beyond itself, so it is not paid back.

parts.note: the classical teller of tales is the Greek epic poet of the Iliad, and a homing pigeon is called by the same name, so the adjective fits both

explanation.surface: A story about a pigeon from ancient times that carried tales.
explanation.walkthrough: Two readings meet: an adjective describing the blind Greek bard of the Iliad, the great teller of tales, and a racing pigeon, which fanciers call a homer.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes anything of or like the Greek epic poet, whose name also means a homing pigeon.

indicators.note: the opening letters of the word history are used, just as an introduction opens a book

explanation.surface: The opening chapter of a history of mankind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Introduction to' takes the first three letters of History; 'of Man' is the possessive, belonging to a man.
explanation.definitionFit: The possessive pronoun means belonging to a male person, the same sense as 'of man'.

explanation.walkthrough: An embalmed Egyptian body is wrapped in linen bandages, and the same word is a child's name for its mother.
explanation.definitionFit: A child's word for its mother, and an embalmed Egyptian corpse swathed in bandages.

clue.text: Gleaner in the first stage of sunburn in Cornwall ?

indicators.note: the gleaner is pictured in red, so her name comes after the colour in the charade

parts.note: sunburn first shows as reddened skin
in the Bible Ruth gleaned barley in the fields of Boaz

explanation.surface: A woman gathering corn in a Cornish field while starting to catch the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruth is the Bible's gleaner, gathering leftover barley in Boaz's fields. Here 'in' means 'dressed in', so the gleaner's name follows the colour rather than going inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A mining town in west Cornwall, so a place located in that county.

clue.text: Ere coots 'come out of the wood

indicators.note: to come out is to emerge in a different form, so the letters of ere coots are rearranged

explanation.surface: Birds emerging from the trees in an old-fashioned rhyme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'come out' (with 'come' cut short in the old style) rearranges ERE COOTS.
explanation.definitionFit: The oily preservative is distilled from wood tar and is painted onto timber, so it comes from wood.

clue.text: Sit uncomfortably between dances with far away looks

indicators.note: the scrambled letters are placed in among the letters of the dances, splitting that word

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: sitting uncomfortably means shifting about, so the letters of sit are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone shifting on a chair between dances, gazing into the distance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncomfortably' rearranges the letters of 'Sit', and 'between' places them after the first letter of 'dances'. 'far away looks' are the far-off parts of a view.
explanation.definitionFit: In painting and in views, the far-off parts of a landscape are its distances, the remote prospects the eye looks towards.

explanation.surface: An exclamation calling a woman a silly owl.
explanation.walkthrough: One definition is a woman's pet name (short for Margaret); the other is an old country name for the barn owl.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name, a form of Margaret, serves as 'she', and in English dialect it is also a name for the barn owl.

clue.text: To run a paper the aspiration of a queen?

parts.note: to run a newspaper is to edit it
an aspiration is a breathed sound, the sound the letter H stands for

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a queen dreams of running a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'aspiration' looks like an ambition, but in phonetics it is the breathy H sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Several English queens bore this name, among them the wife of Edward the Confessor.

parts.note: insects found in the ground grain of a flour mill, named as bugs living in meal

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer's halves literally: bugs in meal, the ground grain a mill produces. The real insects are a sap-sucking garden pest.
explanation.definitionFit: These are scale insects covered in a white powdery wax, and the clue reads them as insects infesting flour.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bag' is the verb: to take something for oneself, as in bagging a seat.
explanation.definitionFit: To bag is to seize for one's own use; the adjective means fitting or proper.

clue.text: Elijah, say, in the matter of that little cloud

definitions.text: Elijah, say, in the matter of that little cloud

parts.words: Elijah, say, in the matter of that little cloud
parts.note: in the Bible Elijah saw a cloud no bigger than a man's hand rise from the sea and foretold heavy rain

explanation.surface: The prophet Elijah looking at a small cloud over the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1 Kings 18 Elijah's servant sees a little cloud rising from the sea, and Elijah warns King Ahab that a downpour is coming, ending the drought.
explanation.definitionFit: Elijah was a biblical seer, and predicting the storm from a tiny cloud made him a forecaster of rain.

clue.text: Sound reinforcement for William when bottled up ?

indicators.note: the clue's first word asks for a phrase that sounds like the answer when spoken

parts.note: help for William of Orange, the Dutch prince who took the English throne in 1688, would be an aid to Orange

explanation.surface: Sending military support to King William in a besieged fortress.
explanation.walkthrough: William III of England was William of Orange, so help sent to him is Orange aid; said out loud that matches a fruit drink sold in bottles.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet fizzy citrus drink is sold in bottles, so bottled up it is a soft drink.

clue.text: Love can't clutch the cup from the man in possession

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O

indicators.note: the word can't grips something inside itself, so another piece goes within it

parts.note: the word written without its apostrophe
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone unable to keep hold of a trophy as its holder takes it back.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is O, from the tennis score. 'clutch' makes 'can't' hold 'the cup' just after its first letter, so the cup sits between C and ANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoever is in possession of a house or seat is its holder or resident.

parts.note: the Corps of ... is a British body of uniformed doormen and porters, many of them ex-servicemen

explanation.walkthrough: 'Officer' and 'Corps' suggest an army officer with a commission; the Corps of Commissionaires is a British organisation, founded 1859, supplying uniformed doormen to hotels, cinemas and offices.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the Corps of Commissionaires is a uniformed doorkeeper, so he wears the uniform of that corps.

clue.text: Macbeth says he's entitled to gas

parts.note: Macbeth, speaking of himself, says me
Macbeth's title was Thane of Glamis, then of Cawdor

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Macbeth claiming a right to talk at length.
explanation.walkthrough: Macbeth is a Scottish thane in the play, so his own words for his rank are 'me thane'. 'gas' looks like idle talk but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Marsh gas, the main part of natural gas, is the simplest hydrocarbon.

annotationWithheld.why: Disallow our lute (4,3): the answer rearranges the letters of 'our lute', yet no clue word signals that shuffle; 'Disallow' is the definition, leaving nothing to act as the anagram signal.

parts.note: reads as a man who usually has children, but an issue is an edition of a newspaper or magazine

explanation.walkthrough: 'issue' reads as children, but it is the edition of a periodical that this person is always preparing.
explanation.definitionFit: The person in charge of a newspaper or journal is always working on the next number of the publication.

parts.note: the Afrikaans name for a foreign settler, chiefly British, in the Boer republic of the Transvaal

explanation.walkthrough: The Transvaal was a Boer republic in southern Africa; the British miners who came for its gold were called by this Afrikaans word for an outlander.
explanation.definitionFit: The Afrikaans word means outlander, a foreigner living in the Boer republic without citizenship.

parts.note: the auctioneer's call suggests a final offer, but a bid can be a farewell bidden as someone departs

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an auction closing; the other reading is the last word one bids to someone who is going away.
explanation.definitionFit: A French farewell, the final goodbye one bids on leaving.

indicators.note: a skater on ice slides and slips about, so the letters of glide slither into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Advice to skate smoothly, like a figure skater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as one on ice' rearranges GLIDE; read whole, the clue also describes the frozen state of someone on ice.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on ice is being chilled, and the adjective means icy cold, frozen.

clue.text: Sailor Bill has one of those early computers

parts.note: AB is an able-bodied seaman
AC is short for account, a bill
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A sailor called Bill owning an old calculating machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sailor Bill' reads as a man's name; it is two pieces, AB and AC.
explanation.definitionFit: Counting frames with beads on wires were the first calculating devices, and the plural form of the word is used here.

clue.text: Not come to point, but to lonely duty perhaps for a policeman down under

definitions.text: lonely duty perhaps for a policeman down under

explanation.surface: An evasive speaker compared with a constable patrolling the empty outback.
explanation.walkthrough: A policeman's round is his beat, and the bush is the Australian back country, so a lonely patrol in the outback is a beat about the bush.
explanation.definitionFit: To avoid coming to the point is the idiom of talking around a subject; literally it is a patrol round in the outback.

parts.note: a scornful exclamation that sounds like the bleat of the sheep in the nursery rhyme Baa, Baa, Black Sheep

explanation.walkthrough: The scornful exclamation is said the same way as a sheep's bleat, as in the nursery rhyme; the black sheep of a family draws contempt.
explanation.definitionFit: A scornful interjection expressing disdain, which also sounds like a sheep's cry.

explanation.walkthrough: A voter marks a cross on the ballot paper; the princes who chose the Holy Roman Emperor held the same title.
explanation.definitionFit: A voter puts a cross on the ballot, and the princes who chose the Holy Roman Emperor held this title.
